children: Logistics are the lifeblood of the economy, and United Parcel Service delivered more than five billion packages in 2025.

When the delivery giant reports third-quarter numbers on Tuesday morning, investors will be looking at how it has dealt with fuel prices and consumer health, and how it sees peak shopping season unfolding.
For the quarter, Wall Street is looking for earnings per share of $1.62 from sales of $22.3 billion. A year ago, UPS reported earnings per share of $1.74 from sales of $21.4 billion.
Sales are expected to grow year over year for the second consecutive quarter. Fuel surcharges will help.

Fuel is generally a pass-through for UPS and much of the logistics industry. Still, higher diesel prices add to costs and can affect shipping patterns. U.S. diesel fuel is about $6.35 per gallon, up from about $3.67 a year ago. Exactly how fuel is impacting customer behavior is a watch item for investors.

UPS is almost done with its Amazon.com "glide down." Almost two years ago, the company announced its plan to walk away from low-profit Amazon business. About two million daily packages left its network.

Now, investors will be looking for operating profit growth in 2027 and beyond, with pressure from lower volumes abated. When operating profit margins will inflect higher at UPS is a "core debate" for investors, according to Bernstein analyst David Vernon.

Despite rising costs for consumers, retail and manufacturing trends remain strong, according to ISI Evercore analyst Jonathan Chappell. Investors hope that strong trends will continue into the fourth quarter.
UPS recently announced plans to hire 100,000 seasonal workers. That's normal for UPS, which is looking to improve on-time performance for holiday shoppers.
How many holiday shoppers it expects will affect more than just UPS stock on Tuesday.
Through Monday trading, UPS stock was up just 1% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 by 11 percentage points.
